name: Unity Catalog
license: Proprietary as a Databricks service; the open-source Unity Catalog server is Apache 2.0
summary: Databricks’ catalog and governance layer for tables, files, functions and models, with managed and external tables, an Iceberg REST endpoint and credential vending; a separate Apache 2.0 open-source server lives at LF AI & Data.
intro: The name covers two things. Most people meet Unity Catalog as the governance layer built into Databricks, on by default for workspaces created after 8 November 2023. There, one metastore per cloud region is shared by the workspaces attached to it, so a grant made in one workspace applies in all of them. Everything you govern is a securable object in a three-level namespace, `catalog.schema.object`: tables, views, volumes (governed folders of non-tabular files under `/Volumes/<catalog>/<schema>/<volume>/`), functions, models and services. Storage credentials, external locations, connections and shares sit directly under the metastore. Access is controlled with `GRANT` and ownership, attribute-based policies on governed tags, per-table row filters and column masks, and workspace bindings, and Unity Catalog records lineage and an audit log as data is used.

Tables and volumes come in two kinds. Managed tables are Databricks’ default and recommendation: Unity Catalog picks where the files go inside a managed storage location in your own cloud account (set on the metastore, catalog or schema), stores them as Delta Lake or, with `USING iceberg`, as Iceberg, and looks after them. Predictive optimization runs `OPTIMIZE`, `VACUUM` and `ANALYZE` on serverless compute, automatic liquid clustering picks clustering keys from your queries, and a dropped managed table’s files are deleted after a recovery period of 7 days by default, during which `UNDROP` brings it back. External tables point at a path you choose inside a registered external location, can also be CSV, JSON, Avro, Parquet, ORC or text, get no automatic optimization, and keep their files when dropped. Foreign tables mirror tables that another catalog, such as a Hive Metastore, AWS Glue or Snowflake Horizon Catalog, still owns, and are read-only. Other engines connect through two open APIs, the Unity REST API for Delta clients and an Iceberg REST catalog at `/api/2.1/unity-catalog/iceberg-rest`, which can read and write managed Iceberg tables and read Delta tables that have Iceberg reads enabled. Both vend short-lived storage credentials that carry the requesting principal’s privileges.

The open-source Unity Catalog is a separate, much smaller implementation. Databricks published it on 12 June 2024 under Apache 2.0 and gave it to the LF AI & Data Foundation, where it is still a sandbox project. It is a Java 17 server with a REST API, a CLI and a web UI that keeps its metadata in H2 by default, with PostgreSQL as an option, and it models the same catalogs, schemas, tables, volumes, functions and models. It added OAuth sign-in, privileges and credential vending for S3, Azure and Google Cloud Storage in 0.2 (September 2024), managed storage locations with experimental managed Delta tables in 0.4 (February 2026), a REST API for catalog-managed Delta commits in 0.5, and views in 0.6 (August 2026). Its Iceberg REST endpoint serves Delta tables with UniForm to Iceberg readers, and its README warns that the APIs are still evolving.
strengths: One permission model for tables, views, volumes, functions and models, with tag-based policies, row filters, column masks, lineage and audit logs, shared by every workspace on the metastore

Managed tables look after themselves: predictive optimization compacts, vacuums and collects statistics, automatic liquid clustering picks keys, and `UNDROP` recovers a dropped table within the recovery period
Open to other engines: Spark, Flink, Trino, DuckDB and other Iceberg REST or Delta clients can read and write managed tables with vended credentials, instead of only reading copies

Governs tables it doesn’t own: catalog federation brings Hive Metastore, Glue and Snowflake Horizon tables under the same grants without moving them, and `SET MANAGED` converts external Delta tables in place
An Apache 2.0 server you can run yourself in Docker, with the same namespace and API shape
limits: Most of the features above are Databricks-only. The open-source server is at 0.x as a sandbox project: its README says the APIs shouldn’t be assumed stable, managed Delta tables are experimental, authorization is off in the default config, and its Iceberg endpoint only serves UniForm tables for reading

Managed tables must be used by name: path-based access isn’t supported (except through Compatibility Mode), creating and writing managed Delta tables from outside Delta clients is in Public Preview, and external Iceberg engines can’t read Unity Catalog views

The automation costs money and setup: predictive optimization needs the Premium plan and bills its runs as serverless jobs, and managed Iceberg tables need serverless compute that can reach your storage

External tables are only governed through Unity Catalog: its grants don’t apply to direct file access, and metadata changed by another client must be synced back with `MSCK REPAIR TABLE … SYNC METADATA`
Foreign tables are read-only (except an internal federated Hive Metastore) and don’t get managed tables’ transactional guarantees or most optimizations

sections.title: Managed and external tables in Databricks SQL
sections.intro: The table lifecycle from Databricks’ documentation. This needs a Databricks workspace, so unlike the snippet above it wasn’t run for this page.
source: -- Managed: Unity Catalog chooses the location and maintains the files
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE main.sales.orders (id BIGINT, amount DECIMAL(10,2))
CREATE TABLE main.sales.refunds (id BIGINT, amount DECIMAL(10,2)) USING iceberg;
-- External: you choose the location, inside a registered external location
CREATE TABLE main.raw.clicks (id BIGINT, url STRING)
DROP TABLE main.raw.clicks;     -- the files in s3://acme-raw/clicks stay
DROP TABLE main.sales.orders;   -- the files go after the recovery period
UNDROP TABLE main.sales.orders; -- ...unless you undo it in time
ALTER SCHEMA main.sales RETAIN DROPPED TO 30 DAYS;
ALTER TABLE main.raw.events SET MANAGED;  -- convert an external Delta table

story: Before Unity Catalog, each Databricks workspace had its own Hive metastore and a separate service for table access controls. Companies with many workspaces had to copy table definitions, views and permissions between them by hand, and the copies drifted. Databricks announced Unity Catalog at its Data and AI Summit in 2021 as one governance layer for data and AI, opened a gated public preview on AWS and Azure in April 2022, and made it generally available later that year (on 25 August 2022 in Azure Databricks). It added a catalog level above Hive’s `database.table`, so the old metastore could show up as one catalog, `hive_metastore`, next to the new ones. From November 2023, new workspaces got Unity Catalog automatically.

In June 2024, about a week after agreeing to buy Tabular, the company founded by Iceberg’s creators, Databricks open-sourced Unity Catalog. It released version 0.1 under Apache 2.0, hosted at the Linux Foundation’s LF AI & Data, with the Iceberg REST catalog API built with Tabular’s expertise and credential vending to gate access to storage. Databricks argued that most platforms were walled gardens and promised that its hosted service implemented the same open APIs.

On the Databricks side, Unity Catalog then took on Iceberg as a first-class format: managed Iceberg tables that outside engines can write through the Iceberg REST API went into public preview in June 2025 and became generally available in May 2026, along with Iceberg v3 and governed access to Iceberg tables in other catalogs. The open-source server has grown more slowly, through 0.x releases that added authentication, storage credentials, managed storage and views.

choices.why: Hive had only databases and tables. A level on top gave data owners more room to organize data and let the existing Hive metastore appear as one catalog, so customers could adopt Unity Catalog alongside it.

choices.choice: One metastore per region, shared by workspaces
choices.why: Per-workspace metastores meant hand-synchronised definitions and permissions. A shared metastore makes a grant in one workspace effective in all workspaces attached to it.

choices.choice: Managed tables in the customer’s own account
choices.why: Unity Catalog decides where managed files go and maintains them, but they stay in the customer’s cloud storage, not Databricks’. That lets Databricks automate layout and cleanup without taking custody of the data.
Other engines can’t be trusted to apply Databricks’ grants, so the catalog checks them and returns short-lived credentials scoped to the table. The same idea underpins the open-source release.
